title.en: Wolf-Boy, the Avenger of Lytton

region.en: Lytton, Fraser-Thompson junction, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 利頓，弗雷澤—湯普森匯流處，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Wolf-Boy' (Thompson, first version)

summary.en: Wolf-Boy, a chief's son reared by his grandmother among the bones of their massacred people, trains in all the arts of his ancestors and gains secret magic power. In a hollow-log canoe he crosses the great lake, his blind grandmother directing the way — 'Open my eyes, child' — until her glance carries the canoe to the far shore. As a wolf he circles the enemy village, becomes a cloud of eagle's down, and sets the whole camp ablaze; only the chief who supplicates him with gifts and his four daughters is spared, and Wolf-Boy marries the daughters, returning at last to Lytton with his wives, children, grandmother and goods.
summary.zh: 酋長之子狼孩與祖母於族人被屠之地相依，習先人百藝，暗得神力。乘空心木舟渡大湖，盲眼祖母引路——『孩子，開我眼』——其目光所及，舟行立至。他化狼繞敵村，化鷹絨雲降火焚營；唯以財禮與四女乞饒之酋長得免。狼孩娶其四女，終攜妻兒祖母財物歸返利頓。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. A second version has the grandmother whip the lake water apart and leap four obstacles by the power of her opened eyes. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Wolf-Boy was an ancestor of the Thompson Indians. He was a chief's son, and lived with his grandmother in a country beyond a great lake. A great war-party of strange people attacked them, and all the people were destroyed except Wolf-Boy and his grandmother, who hid in a hole in the ground. The grandmother reared him and taught him all the arts and knowledge of his people — how to make bow and arrows, how to shoot and how to snare game — until he became a proficient hunter and trapper, killing at last grizzly bears, elk, and all kinds of large animals.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 35-36 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He asked his grandmother who his ancestors were and how it happened that he and she were the only people in that country. She told him that their enemies lived on the other side of the lake. Wolf-Boy wanted to take revenge, and she said, 'You must not think of this. Poor child! You will be killed, and then I shall be all alone.' But he persisted, and she helped him: she told him to hollow out a log like a canoe, and said, 'In this kind of vessel your ancestors travelled on the water.' She appeared blind, but had extraordinary powers of vision — when he opened her eyelids and she looked, the canoe shot forward to the utmost range of her glance, and so they crossed the lake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 36-37 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He left his grandmother and assumed the form of a wolf, circling the enemy village ever nearer. The people saw him and said, 'Look at the wolf that is running round our village!' Suddenly he disappeared, and a small cloud of fine down approached a lodge; when it reached the smoke-hole the house took fire, and soon the whole village was ablaze, the fire pursuing those who tried to escape. The chief ran out, spread a robe, heaped costly things on it, placed his four daughters on top, and supplicated the mystery to stop. The down descended before him and assumed the form of a young man. All the lodges and their people were burned except the chief's. Wolf-Boy lived with the chief, whose daughters became his wives; after four years he went back for his grandmother, whose beautiful piercing eyes the wives opened for her, and thenceforth they lived in his father-in-law's country near Lytton.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 37 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Lytton Girls Stolen by Giants

region.en: Hills near Lytton, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 利頓附近山地，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'The Lytton Girls who were stolen by Giants' (Thompson)

summary.en: Two girls who play too far from camp are carried off under the arms of two giants to their house on an island far down a great river. Kindly treated and fed on game for four years, they are finally taken to a distant huckleberry patch within reach of home — and run. The giants shake the spruce into which they have tied themselves, and try to roll the hollow log they hide in down the hill, but fail both times; the girls reach their people's hunting-camp and tell how the giants — Stsomu'lamux and TsekEtinu's — live and act.
summary.zh: 利頓營地二女貪玩遠行，被二巨人腋下挾走，藏於遠河島上之宅。四年厚待，獵物供食；一年夏，巨人攜之往遠處採越橘，該地離家已近，二女乘隙而逃。巨人搖撼其繫身之雲杉不果，欲滾其藏身之空心木下山亦不果。二女終抵族人獵營，述巨人（名 Stsomu'lamux 與 TsekEtinu's）之居與行。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once some people were camped on the hills near Lytton, and among them were two girls who were fond of playing far away from the camp. Their father warned them against the giants who infested the country. One day they rambled off, and two giants saw them, put them under their arms, and ran off with them to their house on an island in a large river, a long distance away. They treated them kindly and gave them plenty of game to eat — first grouse, rabbits and other small game, then plenty of deer; the girls made much buckskin, and for four years they lived with the giants, who carried them across the river to dig roots and gather berries.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 38-39 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: One summer the giants took them a long distance to a place where huckleberries were very plentiful, left them to gather berries, and went off hunting. The elder sister recognized the place as not many days' travel from their people's home, and they ran away. When about to be overtaken, they climbed into the top of a large spruce and tied themselves with their tump-lines; the giants shook the tree many times and pushed and pulled against it, but it did not break and the girls did not fall, so the giants left. Again pursued, the girls crawled into a large hollow log on a side-hill, closing the openings with branches; the giants tried to pull the branches, peer through the cracks, and roll the log down the hill, but it was too heavy. After a while they left, and the girls ran on until they reached a hunting-camp of their own people in the mountains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 39 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Deer People and the Hunter Who Became a Deer

region.en: Hilly country near Lytton, Thompson lands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 利頓附近丘陵，湯普森人鄉土（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'The Deer' (Thompson, from Upper Thompson and Lytton)

summary.en: A hunter follows doe-tracks to a woman and child and is led underground to the Deer People, who live by killing and reviving one another — the bones thrown into water bring the dead back to life. He marries the Deer-Woman, hunts his brothers-in-law for the people's meat, is transformed into a buck for the rutting-season and becomes its champion. Returning to his own village with compressed bundles of fat and dried meat that expand to feast-mats, he teaches the rule that saves the deer forever: throw the bones into the water so the deer revive and never withhold themselves; and at last the hunter becomes a deer and never returns to the people.
summary.zh: 獵人循母鹿跡遇婦孺，隨之入地底鹿族之鄉。鹿族以互相獵殺為生——骨投於水，死者復活。獵人娶鹿女，為其族人殺鹿取肉；發情季被化為公鹿，竟成季中之雄。攜壓縮脂肉返故里，布一展即成盛宴之席。彼垂訓後世：鹿骨必投水中，鹿乃復活，永不避獵人；最後獵人化鹿而去，不復歸於人間。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Hunting-rite origin (bones to water) — closely tied to ritual practice; published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a man who was a great deer-hunter, always successful; he thought continually of the deer and dreamed of them — they were as friends to him, probably his manitou. One day, following the fresh tracks of a doe and fawn, he came to a knoll where a young woman and child sat, the tracks leading directly to them. She laughed and said, 'You need not trouble yourself about the tracks. For a long time I have loved you and longed for you. Now you shall go with me to my house.' They reached a hilly country, went underground, and found themselves in a large house full of people just like Indians, well dressed in skins and deer-skin robes, amiable and happy. 'Our daughter has brought her husband,' some said.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 40-41 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The people asked their son-in-law to hunt. Two young deer, his brothers-in-law, ran ahead and stood on a knoll; the hunter killed both, cut them up, and carried them home leaving nothing but their manure, for the chief had told him not to throw away any part of the game. The people saved all the bones, wrapped them in bundles, and sent a man to throw them into the water — and the two brothers-in-law and another man came to life when their bones were thrown in. Thus these Deer people lived by hunting and killing each other and then reviving. At the rutting-season the chief put the body of a large old buck on the hunter and transformed him into a buck; younger bucks beat him off and took his wife, until the chief gave him large antlers and the body of a buck in its prime — then he was the champion of the whole season.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 41-42 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In time the Deer-Woman said they should live a while with his people. She compressed a large quantity of deer-fat, dried venison and dressed buckskins to the size of a handful, and the three travelled — transforming themselves into deer when they wished to go fast. At his village the hunter warned that no one must come near him for eight days while he washed in herb decoctions; then his wife threw down the fat on the feast-mats, and it assumed its proper dimensions and covered all the mats, and the people had a feast. In their stays the hunter killed a brother-in-law whenever food was needed and threw the bones into the water, and the deer came back to life; the Deer-Boy taught his half-brother to hunt so that he would never miss, and admonished him always to throw the bones into the water so the deer might revive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 42-43 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Finally they returned toward the Deer people, the Deer-Boy accompanying his half-brother's people to hunt for them on the way, and he never returned — he became an Indian and a great hunter. From him the people learned how to treat deer: 'When you kill deer, always see to it that the bones are not lost. Throw them into the water; then the deer will come to life, and a hunter who does this pleases the deer, who have affection for him and do not keep out of his way. The deer will always remain plentiful, because they are not really killed. If it is impossible to throw the bones into water, then burn them. If a man throws deer-bones about and lets the dogs eat them, the deer will be offended and help him no more; the hunter will have no luck, and will become poor and starve.' The hunter himself never returned to the people; he became a deer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 43 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Boy Who Travelled to the Sun

region.en: Trail to the Sun's house at the edge of the earth (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 通往太陽之屋的大地邊界小徑（象徵定位於利頓）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'The Boy who travelled to the Sun' (Thompson)

summary.en: An ugly chief's son, refused by every girl and mocked as a gambler who has lost everything, steals his mother's clothes and purifies himself in mountain sweat-baths. A dream sends him east to the end of the earth, each day hotter, to the Sun's house, where the Sun's son — the same handsome young man from his dream — receives him. After long companionship in the sky he longs for home, promises to bring women for the Sun and his son, and jumps through the hole scratched in the sky, becoming a star in his descent and a good-looking man on the hill above his village, where the people only say, 'Another star has defecated.'
summary.zh: 醜陋酋長之子求婚皆被拒，又賭輸一切遭人訕笑；竊母衣上山，連沐汗浴淨身。夢中俊美少年囑其東行至大地盡頭，日熱一日，直至太陽之屋；太陽之子（即夢中之人）迎之入內，同遊天界久之。思鄉求歸，許諾為太陽父子携來女子；太陽之子抓破天幕，令其躍下。墜落時化為星，落地成俊男，現身於故村上方山丘；村人見星隕，僅云：『又一顆星大便了。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Sky-journey cycle; the pin is symbolic. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The young man was the son of a chief. He was ugly, and his offers of marriage were refused by all the girls; in consequence he took to playing and became an inveterate gambler, losing all he had, including his clothes. His parents scolded him; the young men and women laughed at him. He became disconsolate, stole some of his mother's clothes, and went to the mountains, where he purified himself in the sweat-bath. He had a dream in which a good-looking young man told him to travel east.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 43-44 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He travelled until he came to a cliff at the far end of the earth, each day growing hotter as he drew near. At last he came to a trail which led to the Sun's house, and met a young man clad in very fine clothes ornamented with suns and stars made of copper, who said he was the Sun's son and had been expecting him — the same man who had appeared in his dream. After the boy had been four days in hiding, the Sun's son told his father about the visitor and asked him not to kill him, for he desired him for a companion. The boy stayed a long time and travelled with the Sun's son in the sky country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 44 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Finally he longed to return home, and told the Sun's son, who did not wish him to leave, saying he would be lonely. The boy promised to return and bring women companions for him and his father, who did not know of women. The Sun's son let him go, scratched a hole through the sky, and told him to jump down. The boy hesitated, but finally obeyed; as he descended he became a star, and on reaching the ground he became a good-looking man, finding himself on a hill above his home village. The people saw the star falling and thought nothing of it, simply saying, 'Another star has defecated.' He opened the tiny bundle the Sun's son had given him and found fine clothes, which assumed their natural size.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 44 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dead Woman and her Child

region.en: Upper Thompson and Lytton villages, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 上湯普森與利頓村落，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'The Dead Woman and her Child' (Thompson)

summary.en: A mother who died days after bearing a daughter returns nightly from the grave to suckle the crying infant, who thrives while the village wonders at the dried milk around its mouth. Two old women watch, and the people prepare medicine, cedar-bark, pitch-wood and four shamans at the four quarters; when the ghost hesitates at the ladder-top and finally descends, they seize her, block every escape above and below, throw medicine on her, and tame her — she becomes like any other woman and quietly suckles her child. Years later, opening a cellar full of mice, she is transformed into one of them and vanishes.
summary.zh: 產女數日即亡之母，夜夜自墳返家哺其啼兒；兒健壯，村人見其口邊乾乳而奇之。二老嫗窺之，族人備藥、雪松皮、松脂薪，四方各置巫師一名。夜半亡者臨梯頂，遲疑良久，終下；四巫擒之，堵其遁地遁天之路，澆藥馴之——她竟復為常人，安然哺乳。數年後開鼠窖，見群鼠竄走，化為其中一鼠而沒。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Ghost-return motif; published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: A woman who had given birth to a daughter died when the child was only a few days old. The people buried the mother and tried to rear the child by feeding it, but the baby was not satisfied and cried. One night, when it was crying after the people had gone to bed and the fire had gone out, the mother came into the house and suckled it, remaining until almost daylight, when she returned to her grave. She did so many nights, and the people wondered that the child thrived so well and did not cry during the night, and noticed in the morning the dried milk around its mouth and other signs that it had been suckled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 44 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: They asked two old women to watch. About midnight the child cried, and her mother approached, calling her child in a low voice, descended the ladder, lay down with it, and stayed until near daybreak. The people prepared to capture her: they boiled medicine in a large bucket, tore up dry cedar-bark to make a blaze, covered the fire with ashes to keep it alive, had split pitch-wood ready, and placed four shamans at the north, south, east and west. At midnight she came to the top of the ladder and hesitated a long time, seeming to know something was wrong; but when her baby continued to cry she climbed down, and the four shamans seized her and held her fast. She tried to escape by going underground and into the air, but the shamans blocked her passage at every point; others lighted a bright fire and threw medicine on her, until at last she was tamed — her struggles ceased, and she became like any other woman, lying down quietly to suckle her child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 44-45 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some years after this, when her daughter was grown up, they went together to bring food from their cellar. The girl sat at the entrance while the mother opened the cellar and looked in: it was full of mice, which scampered about in every direction. While she was looking at the mice, she became transformed into one of them and finally disappeared among them. The girl sat outside and cried because her mother had become a mouse, and the people took her home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 45 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Holholakwo'xa, the Man Who Filed His Feet

region.en: Thompson villages, British Columbia (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 湯普森村落，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位於利頓）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Holholakwo'xa or Holakwo'xa' (Thompson)

summary.en: A fat, silent old man who picks lice all day and covers his legs from every visitor is secretly filing them to points as sharp as awls. One night he stabs the whole sleeping lodge; the young man of the next lodge warns his people, and when Holakwo'xa attacks them awake, a fight ends with the killer's sharp foot stuck fast in the lodge-post — both feet wedged — and the young man with the war-knife slays him and throws him to the dogs.
summary.zh: 肥碩寡言之老者終日捉蝨，見客必掩其足；實則暗自磨腿，銳利如錐。一夜刺殺全屋熟睡之人。鄰屋青年警覺告眾；翌夜霍拉科瓦來襲，眾人已醒，混戰中其銳足插入屋柱，雙足皆嵌，青年持戰刀殺之，棄屍於犬。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Monster-slayer episode; published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Holakwo'xa was an old man who lived with the people. He was very fat, had long hair, and spent most of his time picking lice from his head; he seldom spoke to any one. Sometimes he would turn his back to the people, and they could hear the noise of filing. When any one came to see him, he covered up his legs; when they wanted to see his feet, he pulled them under him and wrapped his robe around himself, saying, 'No, I am afraid you would shoot my feet if I were to show them.' Nevertheless some of the people discovered that he was filing his legs and feet, and thought he was demented. At last his legs were as sharp as awls.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 46 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: One night he arose and stabbed all the people in the lodge while they were asleep. A young man who visited the lodge the following day asked how the people had died, and Holakwo'xa replied that a war-party had killed them. The young man warned the people of the neighboring lodge to be watchful. That night Holakwo'xa entered their lodge, found they were not asleep, and attacked them, jumping and kicking; a fight ensued, and he killed many. The young man, armed with a large war-knife, attacked him, dodged his kicks, and Holakwo'xa's foot stuck fast in the post of the underground lodge; kicking with his other leg to free himself, that leg stuck fast also. The young man then slew him and threw him outside to the dogs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 46 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Peqo's el ea'pi.la: The Sister Who Searched Beyond the Mountains

region.en: From the Thompson country east across the Rocky Mountains (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自湯普森故地東越落基山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Peqo's el ea'pi.la' (Thompson, from Spences Bridge)

summary.en: A man and his younger sister love each other; the people kill the man and, carrying his body east across many mountains, leave it on an islet in a lake of the plains, then settle far off where game abounds, sure the girl can never find them. Distracted with grief, she dreams of the body and receives shaman's power; she crosses the mountains alone, living by snaring and fishing, calling her brother 'Peqo's el ea'pi.la' as she weeps, builds a raft to the islet, and after four days of shaman treatment brings him back to life. They live as husband and wife, and their descendants, the Thompson say, are their relatives east of the Rocky Mountains.
summary.zh: 兄妹相愛，族人殺兄棄屍——越諸山東行，置屍於平原湖中小島，遷居獵豐之遠地，自謂其妹永不復尋。妹悲痛欲絕，夢中見兄屍所在，遂得巫力；獨自越山，捕獵為生，一路泣呼兄名『Peqo's el ea'pi.la』；紮筏渡至小島，以巫術療之四日，兄復活。二人結為夫婦，子孫相承——湯普森人自謂落基山以東即有此親戚。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Sibling-union tale of a type recorded in the ethnographic literature; presented plainly as collected. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: A man fell in love with his younger sister, and she reciprocated his affection. Some of the people prepared to desert the infatuated couple, while others wanted to kill them; finally they killed the man and deserted the girl, carrying the body of the youth along. After travelling far eastward and crossing many mountains, including the Rocky Mountains, they came to a flat prairie with many lakes; in one of these was an islet, and here they deposited the man's remains. Then they settled about a day's journey farther east, in a country of low hills, meadows and lakes, where buffalo, antelope and other game were plentiful, saying, 'The girl can never find us here, and she will never find her lover's remains.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 47 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the girl realized what had happened, she became distracted with grief, travelling about many days and nights not knowing what she was doing. At last, in a dream, she saw the body of her brother on the islet in the lake; in many dreams she received inspiration and advice, became a shaman, and knew what the people had done and where they had gone. She made clothes and moccasins and travelled eastward following the way the people had gone, living by shooting and snaring game and by fishing, often weeping as she went and addressing her brother, 'Peqo's el ea'pi.la.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 47 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When she reached the lake, her clothes and shoes ragged and patched, she made a canoe (or raft) and crossed to the islet. She treated her brother's body as shamans do, and after four days he came back to life. They lived together as husband and wife and had children; after some years, people who went to the lake found him living there with his sister, were afraid, and moved farther east. The brother and sister continued to live at this place, and their descendants are said to live there now, east of the Rocky Mountains. None of the other people returned to their original home; therefore the Thompson say that they have relatives east of the Rocky Mountains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 47-48 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Migration Legend: Crossing the Frozen Lake

region.en: From beyond a great lake to the Thompson country at Lytton (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自大湖彼岸遷至利頓湯普森故地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Migration Legend' (Thompson)

summary.en: Hemmed in beside a great lake by enemies who will destroy them, the people hold a council and dance; shaman after shaman shows his power — men swim like beavers, but none can carry the whole tribe across. At last two chiefs contend: one calls up heat until the people take to the water; the other, dancing and singing, brings a cold wind, and that night ice covers the lake. At daybreak the tribe crosses, and the heat chief melts the ice behind them so the enemy cannot follow. They move camp four times — once lacking wood, once bark, once fish, once game — until they reach the country where everything is plentiful: the Thompson country at Lytton, where they became the ancestors of the Thompson Indians.
summary.zh: 族人被敵圍於大湖之畔，瀕臨滅頂；遂聚議共舞。巫者接連顯能——有人如水獺善泳，然無人能渡舉族。最後二酋相競：一酋召熱，人皆下水乘涼；一酋歌舞召寒風，當夜湖面結冰。黎明舉族踏冰而過，熱酋復召熱風融冰，敵不得追。其後四遷其營——缺薪、缺樹皮、缺魚、缺獸各一次——終至水陸百物豐饒之地：利頓之湯普森故土，湯普森人由此而生。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Boas notes the tale's resemblance to the Exodus crossing and to later tribal displacements. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: A long time ago the people were living in another country, near a large lake, where they were attacked by enemies. Since they could not cross the water, they were hemmed in by their enemies and in danger of being destroyed. Their two chiefs called the men together for a council and dance. One after another the shamans and other men danced and sang, calling up their manitous and soliciting aid; each man showed his powers, and some accomplished wonderful deeds. Some could swim like beavers and otters, and might have crossed the lake, but they could not convey the whole tribe across. On the following day they expected the attack of their enemies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 48 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some people went into the sweat-houses to purify themselves and pray; others joined in a war-dance preparing for battle. Only the two chiefs had not yet shown their powers. They contended with each other: one had power over heat, the other over cold. When one called up his powers, it became so hot that the people took to the water to cool themselves — still they saw no way of escape. Then the other chief danced and sang, and a cold wind began to blow; the people fled to their lodges and lighted fires. That night ice covered the lake, and at daybreak the tribe crossed to the other side. Then the chief whose guardian-spirit was heat caused a hot wind to blow, the ice disappeared, and their enemies could not follow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 48-49 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yet the people thought, 'Even here our enemies may follow us,' and travelled still farther away. They camped for a time, but four times they moved, dissatisfied — one place had an insufficiency of wood, another of bark, another of fish, another of game. At last they came to a country where wood, bark, fish, and game were plentiful, and there they remained: the Thompson country at Lytton. They became the ancestors of the Thompson Indians. On their journey they crossed a great lake, a great plain, a great forest, and a great mountain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 49 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Woman Who Became a Horse

region.en: Open plains of the Thompson-Okanagon border (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 湯普森—奧卡諾根交界平原（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'The Woman who became a Horse' (Thompson/Okanagon)

summary.en: A chief's wife who rides his fine stallion grows careless of her household and enamoured of the horse, which sniffs about her as stallions do with mares; when her husband learns the truth he shoots the stallion, and at daybreak she is gone. A year later the people find her among a band of wild horses, partly transformed — a mane of long hair, a tail of grown body hair, arms and legs changed, but the face still human. Run down and lassoed, she is brought home, watched, and tries in vain to be tamed, whinnying like a horse, until they set her free; the next year she is almost entirely horse, with a colt at her side, and has many children afterwards.
summary.zh: 酋長之妻常騎其駿馬，漸荒家務、迷戀此馬；馬嗅其身如嗅母馬。夫知情後射殺雄馬，妻黎明失蹤。一年後，族人於野馬群中見她——髮化鬃，體毛化尾，肢體已變，唯面尚人形。追捕套縛帶回，欲馴之，她馬嘶不止，終被縱歸。翌年再見，幾全化為馬，身側有駒，其後生駒眾多。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson/Okanagon narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: A chief had many horses, and among them a stallion which his wife often rode. The woman and stallion became enamoured of each other and cohabited. The woman grew careless of her household duties, and always wanted to look after the horses. When the people moved camp and the horses were brought in, it was noticed that the stallion made right for the woman and sniffed about her as stallions do with mares; after this she was watched. When her husband learned the truth, he shot the stallion. The woman cried and would not go to bed; at daybreak she was gone, no one knew where.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 53 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: About a year after this it was discovered that she had gone off with some wild horses. One day when the people were travelling over a large open place, they saw a band of horses and the woman among them. She had partly changed into a horse: her hair had grown so long that it resembled a tail, she had much hair on her body, the hair of her head resembled a horse's mane, and her arms and legs had changed considerably — but her face was still human and bore some resemblance to her original self. The chief sent young men to chase her; all the wild horses ran away, but she could not run so fast and was run down and lassoed. She was brought into her husband's lodge, and the people watched her for some time, trying to tame her, but she continued to act and whinny like a horse; at last they let her free. The following year they saw her again: she had become almost entirely horse, and had a colt by her side. She had many children afterwards.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 53 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Orphans Who Ascended to Heaven

region.en: White Man's country, then the road to the land of the dead (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 白人之鄉，後至亡者之路（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'The Orphans who ascended to Heaven' (Thompson)

summary.en: Two orphaned brothers, whose village a thunder-storm destroyed, are adopted by the childless chief of a town of adult men. The elder, given a saddle-horse that can run around the edge of the earth in two hours, follows the chief's cattle to a road like a mown swath and over the hill into the land where the dead leave their belongings, where the chief who meets the dead warns him: only the dead can stay. He is shown two houses — one of quarrelling sinners living on raw reptile flesh under a Devil cutting up frogs, and one of singing, praying, clean-dressed souls where none may enter unless pure in body and mind. Back home, the whole people set out in procession for that land; but one by one, as each thinks of what he left behind, he becomes a crow, snake, bird, animal, reptile or insect — until only the chief and the two boys arrive, the only mortals who live in heaven.
summary.zh: 雷雨滅村，二孤兒投奔無子之酋長，被收為養子。兄獲神駿，兩時辰可環行大地一周；其逐牛蹤至如刈草帶之大道，越嶺入亡者棄物之鄉。接引亡者之酋長告之：唯死者可留。乃示以兩屋：一屋內罪人相鬥，以生爬蟲之肉為食，魔首於前切蛙；一屋內歌禱之人，衣著潔淨，然非身心純淨者不得入。歸而告眾，舉族列隊往之；途中人人思念塵世舊物，逐一化為鴉、蛇、鳥、獸、蟲——最後唯酋長與二童抵達，成為唯一以凡身居天堂之人。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Teit notes this tale shows strong missionary influence and a fusion of Indian and Christian ideas — noted here as part of the record's collection history. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Somewhere in the White Man's country there was a populous village. Two brothers belonging to this place strayed away playing and did not return until late in the evening; meanwhile a thunder-storm destroyed the village and killed the people. When the boys returned they found nothing but smoking ruins, and said, 'Our parents and relatives have been killed. There is nobody left here. Let us go away!' After some days they arrived starving at a town in a hollow, where the people were all adult men — neither women nor children. They stole bread and meat from the chief's pig-pen, were caught, questioned, and adopted by the childless chief, who told his cook to feed them on the best. They swept floors, carried wood and water, and grew fast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 53-54 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the chief let the elder boy choose one of his eight exactly alike bay horses, and the boy chose correctly the one that could run around the edge of the earth in two hours, and then chose its own saddle and bridle — so the chief knew he was gifted with magic. Told to herd the cattle on a far hillside, the boy followed their tracks into rough country and found a wide road, as if lately mown, leading up between steep open slopes. Following it over the hill he came to another country, beautiful as mountain-tops, where the dead people left their earthly belongings in great piles; just over the hill a gold staff stood in the ground. The chief who meets the dead and admits them to their places in spirit-land appeared suddenly and told him, 'You are a living being and cannot stay here. Only people who have died can stay here.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 54-55 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: But, seeing that he had come, the guide showed him things to tell on earth. He unlocked two houses: in one the people quarrelled and fought, reptiles crawling among them, living on raw reptile flesh, their chief — the Devil — sitting with a huge frog before him, cutting up pieces of flesh like a butcher. In the other house the people ranged as far as the eye could see, all singing and praying, some on their knees praising God, all with hair of the same length: 'No one can enter there unless he is pure in body and mind. A person must have no sins, and no thoughts of earth and earthly things.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 55 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Back home, the chief called his people together to go in a body to the new land the boy had discovered. The boy warned him, 'You are wealthy here, and it is hard to go there: you have to forget everything on earth and think only of good and heaven.' The people formed a procession, soldiers marching ahead, the chief and the two boys driving behind in the chief's buggy. At last one by one, as each thought of what he had left behind, they became transformed into crows or snakes, which flew or crawled away — into birds, animals, reptiles, and insects — until none were left but the chief and the two boys. These three reached the other land and remained there: they are the only people with mortal bodies who live in heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 55-56 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Ai'lul the Unlucky Gambler

region.en: Mountain sweat-lodges above the Thompson villages (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 湯普森村落山中之汗屋（象徵定位於利頓）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Ai'lul; or, The Unlucky Gambler' (Thompson)

summary.en: Warned against gambling and always losing, Ai'lul ('Loser') gambles away his clothes and his mother's only blanket; she shames him by wrapping her kilt around his neck, and he lies in a corner refusing even a pitying girl's robe. He takes mat, basket, fire-drill and knife to the mountains, sweating four days in each of four sweat-lodges and training for years while his people think him dead. Returning with knowledge of games, he wins from every player — even the best gamblers — wins much property, and refuses every girl until the beautiful daughters of Loon and Swan, good singers and flute-players, become his wives.
summary.zh: 艾盧爾（意為『輸家』）屢賭屢輸，竟連衣物與其母唯一之毯皆輸光；母以己裙圍其頸以羞之，他臥於屋角，連憐憫少女所贈之袍亦拒。攜席、籃、鑽火器、小刀上山，四座汗屋各沐四日，苦練多年，族人皆以為其已死。藝成而返，逢賭必勝，雖高手亦敗；贏得大量財物。眾女求嫁皆拒，直至潛鳥與天鵝之美人二女自薦——善歌善笛——遂娶為妻。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: A young man was warned by his parents and relatives against gambling; he always lost. One day he gambled away all his clothes and his mother's only blanket. She was angry at him and, in order to put him to shame, took off her kilt and wrapped it around his neck. He was very much ashamed, and lay down in a corner of the lodge; a young girl pitied him and offered him a robe, but he refused it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 56 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: At night he took a mat, a basket, a fire-drill, and a knife, and went off to the mountains. He built a sweat-lodge in which he remained four days, then moved to another place and sweated four more days; the fourth sweat-lodge he made quite large and lived in it, training himself for a long time — according to some informants, for four years. His people thought he had committed suicide. When he had gained knowledge regarding games, he returned home. The men with whom he had formerly played said, 'Loser has returned. Let us play with him!' Urged on, he played, his mother giving him a robe and her ear-rings to start. He gained from every one who played with him; the best gamblers tried him, but all lost, and he won much property.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 56 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then all the girls wanted to marry him; but he refused them all, until the beautiful daughters of Loon and Swan came and offered themselves, their mothers bringing them. Ai'lul's mother accepted them, and when he agreed, they became his wives. They were good singers, and could play well on flutes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 56 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Man Who Married Cold's Daughter

region.en: Beyond the farthest snowy range, home of the Cold people (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 極北雪山之外，寒族之鄉（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'The Man who married Cold's Daughter' (Thompson)

summary.en: A poor young man rides away to seek adventures and falls in with a white prospector who plots to have him kill his own last horse as eagle-bait for the gold ledge; when the promised revival of the horse fails, the Eagles whisper that the gold belongs to his grandmother on the plain, carry him to her, and she arms him with a golden staff against the tests of the Cold. He wins the Ice-seat trial, digs the unfreezing spring, makes the duck-lake that will not freeze, builds the stone corral of all animals, and picks his bride by her wink among the identical sisters. Fleeing home with wife and child, they escape the pursuing Cold mother as lake, ducks, old man and church; then Cold himself comes on, freezing the Heat people in their house, until old Heat draws the Chinook wind from his bag and thaws the world. Cold is defeated, granted one short yearly visit to his daughter — and that is winter; his son-in-law throws the golden staff into the river, and since then gold shows in the sand after a Chinook wind has blown.
summary.zh: 貧少年獨騎遠行，遇白人礦工誘其殺最後一匹馬為餌取崖上之金；馬屍無法復活，神鷹告之：金本屬其平原祖母，遂載之往。祖母授金杖以抗寒族諸試煉。他坐冰座而不僵，開不凍之泉，造不凍鴨湖，築石欄收百獸，並於雙生姊妹中憑其眨眼認出新娘。偕妻兒出逃，途中屢化——湖與鴨、老翁與朽屋、教堂與主教——騙退寒母；寒神親追，熱族幾乎凍斃，老熱神自囊中放出欽諾克暖風，天地回春。寒神敗退，獲准歲末探女一回——是為冬季。女婿將金杖投河，自此欽諾克風後，河沙易見金光。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Teit notes the tale combines Plateau, Plains, and European elements. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a young man who felt very bad because he had become very poor, with just one horse left. He made up his mind to seek adventures and rode away. Passing below a high cliff he saw a white man walking in front of a cabin, who shouted, 'Do you see the gold up there in the cliff, where the eagles nest?' Coarse gold and nuggets lay scattered over a shelf of the rock. 'Get the gold, and let us divide it!' said the white man: 'Kill your horse, cut it open, hide by its side, and when the two eagles come, seize their legs; they will fly with you up to where the gold is.' The Indian agreed for the promised revival of the horse, killed and opened it, and hid. Coyote, Wolf, Magpie and others gathered to feed on the body, and when the two eagles alighted he seized them by the legs and was flown up to the ledge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 57-58 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The white man spread four blankets and shouted, 'Gather the gold and throw it down upon the blankets!' — 'You have not yet revived my horse,' said the Indian; the man gathered the scattered bones and tried, but the horse would not come to life. The Eagles spoke: 'Do not speak to the white man. He cares for nothing but gold. The gold belongs to the old woman, your grandmother, who lives out on the plain; she left it here in the mountains, and we are its keepers.' They carried him far off to her lodge, where he stayed long and gained much knowledge from his grandmother, who had four sons that went out every day and returned at night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 58 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He pined for a wife, and his brothers said the only fine girls they had seen lived at the other end of the earth: the two daughters of the Cold, but no one could go there and return alive. His grandmother gave him her golden staff — 'When you sit down, put it under you. It will prevent you from freezing, and will keep you warm' — and her Eagle servants carried him beyond the farthest snowy range to the three houses of the Cold. He entered the younger daughter's house and asked her to marry him; she set him on a block of ice expecting him to freeze, but his seat seemed luminous and turned to gold. She chose him for her husband, warning: 'My father will test you. Think only of me; call me up, saying, O my wife! I seek your help! and I shall be there to help you, although unseen.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 58-59 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Cold set the tasks: the man dug a ditch by drawing a line along the ground so the spring followed behind him, and a warm creek ran past Cold's door through the hardest frost; he spread his arms and made the great duck-lake that would not freeze; he described a circle and a stone enclosure appeared, and a wider circle brought all kinds of animals which he drove into the corral; and he picked out his bride correctly by the wink among the exactly alike sisters. 'You have performed all the tasks. Now you are my son-in-law.' In each sister's house a flute played by itself — loudly when they were home, faintly when they were out, silent when they were far — so they could not go away undiscovered; but after two years the boy cried for his grandparents, and they left, the flute kept playing by the husband's command.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 59-60 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Cold's wife pursued them, but the girl transformed her husband into an old duck, the child into a duckling and herself into a lake; then into a gray-headed bent old man and an old decayed log-house; then the child into a priest, the husband into a bishop and herself into a church. So Cold went himself — 'If you go, you will kill everything, even our daughter.' The north wind blew with snow-storms, ice formed around the house of the Heat people, and all were about to die, until old Heat drew the Chinook wind from the bag at his right side; the air became warm, the ice melted, and the people revived. Heat said, 'I have overcome you. You shall return to your country and live there. Your daughter shall not go back.' Cold pleaded to come once a year and see her for a short time, and the Heat chief agreed: therefore Cold now comes once a year, and then it is winter. Heat-Man threw the staff into the river, and since then gold has been in the rivers — more easily seen after a Chinook wind has blown.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 60-62 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote Goes Fishing: The Frozen Tail

region.en: Frozen river, Shuswap country (symbolic pin at Kamloops)
region.zh: 結冰之河，舒什瓦普故地（象徵定位於坎盧普斯）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Coyote goes Fishing' (Shuswap)

summary.en: Fox sits on a beaver-hole in the ice and lets Coyote believe he is fishing with his tail; Coyote begs the spot, Fox warns him not to give up if the fish don't bite, and slips away to raise a cold wind that freezes Coyote's tail fast. Beaver comes and releases him. (In another telling, Coyote tricks Fox into the hole and freezes him, until Fox calls his own guardian-spirit the Chinook Wind, frees himself with lumps of ice rattling on his tail, and chases Coyote — who escapes through a second hole, leaving his excrements talking by the first to deceive the waiting Fox until they dry up.)
summary.zh: 狐狸坐於冰上河貍洞口，令郊狼誤以為其以尾釣魚。郊狼央求換位，狐囑耐心，隨後召寒風凍住郊狼之尾，河貍前來解救。另一異文：郊狼騙狐入洞凍之；狐呼其守護靈欽諾克風自解，尾上冰塊鏗然，追擊郊狼；郊狼自另一洞口遁走，留其糞便代為說話，狐枯坐等待，至糞乾聲止方知受騙。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Shuswap narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: One time in winter, Fox saw Coyote coming, and sat down on a beaver-hole in the ice. Coyote asked him what he was doing, and Fox said he was fishing with his tail. Coyote thought he would like to have some fish, and asked Fox to let him fish; Fox agreed, told him not to get tired if the fish did not bite at first — he would certainly catch many in time — and left. Then Fox later caused a cold wind to come, and Coyote's tail froze in the hole. Coyote called for help, and Beaver came and released him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 62 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Others say that Coyote induced Fox to put his tail into the hole, then caused a cold wind to come — Cold was one of his guardian-spirits — and Fox was frozen in. When Fox discovered that Coyote had fooled him, he called the Chinook Wind, who was his guardian-spirit, and released himself, then pursued Coyote with lumps of ice rattling on his tail. Coyote ran into a hole with another outlet; he defecated and ordered his excrements to talk while he made his escape. Fox remained sitting by the hole, thinking Coyote was still there; but finally the excrements dried up and ceased talking, and then Fox knew that Coyote had cheated him, and went away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 62 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Hunter Who Fooled the Grizzly Bear

region.en: Botani Valley, Thompson country (symbolic pin at Lytton)
region.zh: 博塔尼谷，湯普森人故地（象徵定位於利頓）

texts.period: Collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'The Hunter who fooled the Grizzly Bear' (Thompson, from Spences Bridge)

summary.en: Travelling unarmed in Botani Valley, a man meets a large grizzly with no way of escape and lies down on his back feigning death; the bear growls and threatens to strike, but he never moves or breathes, until she takes him for dead and goes away after her cubs. In the version told of the hunter Naukawi'lEx, warned by an old man's bad dream, he carried only a knife; the bear stood over him with raised paw, smelled him all over, felt him with its paw, turned him over — and he remained quite rigid, and was not even scratched.
summary.zh: 博塔尼谷中，手無寸鐵之人遇巨熊，退無可退，遂仰臥詐死。熊低吼威嚇，舉爪欲擊，其人屏息不動；熊以為其已死，遂領幼崽而去。另有異文：獵人 Naukawi'lEx 因老者惡夢示警僅携小刀出行；熊立其上，爪高舉，遍嗅其身，以爪撫之，翻轉其體——其人僵直如木，熊竟未傷其分毫。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Thompson narrative recorded by Teit and published by Boas & Teit, 1917; not verbatim. The narrator classed the second version as historical fact rather than myth; both tellings are given as collected. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: A man was travelling in Botani Valley, and saw a large grizzly bear approaching. He saw no way of escape and, being unarmed, thought he would feign death. He lay down on his back, and when the bear came to smell him, he held his breath. The bear threatened to strike him and growled, but he never moved. At last the bear, thinking the man was dead, went away (following her cubs, some say).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 63 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the other telling, a hunter from Spences Bridge camped in Botani Valley; an old man told him to be careful when he hunted that morning, as he had had a bad dream about a grizzly bear. The hunter carried no weapon except a knife; suddenly, when he turned a bend in the trail, he saw a large silver-tip grizzly and was unable to get away unobserved. Remembering his grandfather's advice — in such a case, lie perfectly still and hold the breath — he threw himself on the trail and remained quite still. The bear approached cautiously, stood over him with its paw raised ready to strike, then lowered it, smelled him all over, felt of him with its paw, and turned him over; the hunter remained quite rigid, and the bear went away, evidently believing that he was mysterious. He was not even scratched.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 63-64 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Old-One and the Earth, Our Mother

region.en: Okanagon and Sanpoil country, Washington (symbolic pin at Okanogan River)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根與桑普瓦故地，華盛頓州（象徵定位於奧卡諾根河）

texts.period: Told by Red-Arm (Nespelim/Lower Okanagon); collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 2. Old-One' (Okanagon, told by Red-Arm)

summary.en: Old-One, or Chief, made the earth out of a woman, saying she would be the mother of all the people; the earth is alive yet — the soil her flesh, trees and vegetation her hair, rocks her bones, the wind her breath. She shivers and contracts in cold, expands and perspires in heat, and when she moves we have an earthquake. From her flesh Old-One rolled balls of mud and transformed them into the beings of the ancient world, people and yet animals, each powerful in some ways and helpless in others, many of them cannibals who could not tell people from deer; his last balls, shaped like Indians, he blew upon, and they became alive — the most helpless of all created things, whom the monsters preyed upon. When evil still prevailed, the Chief sent Coyote to earth to destroy the monsters, make life easier, and teach the people the best way to do things.
summary.zh: 老者（即主神）以一女子之身造大地，並言其為萬民之母。大地至今有靈：土壤為其肉，草木為其髮，巖石為其骨，風為其息。寒則顫慄收縮，熱則舒展汗出；其動則地震生。老者取其肉搓為泥丸，化為上古生靈——亦人亦獸，各有其能亦各有其弱，多為食人者，人獸不分。最後所搓者形似印第安人，吹氣而活——乃受造物中最弱者，遂為怪物所噬。世間仍多惡，主神乃遣郊狼下凡，誅怪獸、濟眾生、授民以術。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon/Nespelim narrative told by Red-Arm and recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. The informant also told a Garden-of-Eden/Jesus episode under missionary influence, noted here as collection context but not treated as a separate Plateau record. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Old-One, or Chief, made the earth out of a woman, and said she would be the mother of all the people. Thus the earth was once a human being, and she is alive yet; but she has been transformed, and we cannot see her in the same way we can see a person. Nevertheless she has legs, arms, head, heart, flesh, bones, and blood: the soil is her flesh; the trees and vegetation are her hair; the rocks, her bones; and the wind is her breath. She lies spread out, and we live on her. She shivers and contracts when cold, and expands and perspires when hot. When she moves, we have an earthquake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 80 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Old-One, after transforming her, took some of her flesh and rolled it into balls, as people do with mud or clay, and transformed them into the beings of the ancient world, who were people, and yet at the same time animals. Some could fly like birds and others swim like fishes; all had greater powers and were more cunning than either animals or people — but not well balanced: each was exceedingly wise in some things and exceedingly foolish in others. As a rule they were selfish, there was much trouble among them, and some were cannibals who lived by eating one another: they knew they had to live by hunting, but did not know which beings were people and which deer, and thought people were deer and preyed on them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 80-81 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Old-One made each ball of mud a little different from the others, and rolled them over and over, shaping them and making them alive. The last balls he made were almost all alike and different from any of the preceding ones: they were formed like Indians, and he called them men. He blew on them, and they became alive. They were Indians, but were ignorant and knew no arts — the most helpless of all things created, and the cannibals and other monsters preyed on them particularly. The people and animals were made male and female so that they might breed; thus everything living sprang from the earth, and when we look around we see everywhere parts of our mother. The Chief then sent Coyote to earth to destroy all the monsters and evil beings, to make life easier and better for the people, and to teach them the best way to do things.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 81-82 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote Sent to Set the World in Order

region.en: Okanagon and Sanpoil country, Washington (symbolic pin at Okanogan River)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根與桑普瓦故地，華盛頓州（象徵定位於奧卡諾根河）

texts.period: Told by Red-Arm (Nespelim/Lower Okanagon); collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, 1. Coyote' (Okanagon, told by Red-Arm)

summary.en: Chief saw that the people were having a hard time, preyed upon by many evil beings and about to be killed off; not wanting them exterminated, he sent Coyote to help them — endowing him with great magical power to surmount all obstacles, with power to transform evil beings, and with wisdom and cunning, and giving even Coyote's excrements power to be his friends and advisers. He told him to travel all over the world and set it right, adding that when Coyote's work was finished, he would meet him, see his work, and then give him a rest.
summary.zh: 主神見民困苦，備受諸惡所噬，行將滅絕；不欲其亡，乃遣郊狼相助：授以大神力可越一切險阻，賜其變形諸惡之權，并賜智慧狡計；甚至其糞便亦得言語，為其友與謀士。命其周行天下，整飭其間；並許諾功成之日，將親見其業，而後許其休息。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon/Nespelim narrative told by Red-Arm and recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was sent by Chief to set the world in order. Chief saw that the people were having a hard time and were preyed upon by many evil beings; they were about to be killed off. Chief did not want the people to be exterminated, so he sent Coyote to help them. He endowed him with great magical power, so that he could surmount all obstacles; he gave him power to transform evil beings, and he gave him wisdom and cunning. He also gave to Coyote's excrements the power to be his friends and advisers. He told him to travel all over the world and to set it right. Coyote had to travel much and to work hard. Chief said that when Coyote's work was finished, he would meet him, see his work, and then give him a rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 65 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Origin of the Columbia River: Coyote and the Dripping Water
title.zh: 哥倫比亞河之起源：郊狼與滴水

region.en: Dry coulee that became the Columbia River, Washington (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 乾涸峽谷，後成哥倫比亞河，華盛頓州（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Red-Arm (Nespelim/Lower Okanagon); collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (2a) Origin of the Columbia River' (Okanagon, told by Red-Arm)

summary.en: Hearing water drip, Coyote mimics it four times — 'Hox-hox-hox-hox!' — and, angered that the noise never ceases, kicks the dripping place and laughs that no more water shall drip. But the water follows him, growing in volume as it flows; on the dry plateau he grows thirsty, and each time he descends to drink the creek has become a larger stream behind him. Driven to walk, then wade, then swim with his mouth close to the water, he drinks so much that he loses consciousness — and thus, from a few drops, the Columbia River originated.
summary.zh: 郊狼聞滴水聲，四度模仿『霍霍霍霍』而不得其靜，怒而踢水滴之處，笑曰：『吾已勝汝，水不得復滴作響。』然水銜尾而至，愈流愈盛；於乾燥高地上，郊狼屢渴屢下飲，每次下望，溪已成河。最後涉水而泳，口貼水面暢飲，竟致不省人事——區區滴水，遂成哥倫比亞大河。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon/Nespelim narrative told by Red-Arm and recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Landscape etiology for the Columbia; the pin marks the dry coulee of the tale. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and heard water dropping. He said, 'I will go and beat it.' He sat down near it and cried, 'Hox-hox-hox-hox!' in imitation of water dripping. He tried four times, but the noise never ceased. He became angry, arose, and kicked the place where the water dropped; the noise ceased. He thought he had beaten it, and laughed, saying, 'I beat you. No more shall water drip thus and make a noise.' Shortly after he had gone, the water began to drip as before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 65-66 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He became angry: 'Did I not say water shall not run and make a noise?' The water was coming after him, and increased in volume as it flowed. He kept on running, still hearing the noise of water, and travelled along the edge of a plateau where there was no water nor trees, and everywhere below the coulee was dry. It was warm, and he became very thirsty; looking down into the coulee he saw a small creek, went down, and drank his fill — but had barely reached the top again when he was thirsty once more, and the creek below had grown. The more he drank, the sooner he became thirsty again; the fourth time the water had risen to a good-sized river close by.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 66 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'What may be the matter? I am always thirsty now. There is no use of my going away. I will walk along the edge of the water' — and still thirsty, 'I will walk in the water.' It reached up to his knees; he walked deeper, to the waist, then to the arms. Then he said, 'I will swim, so that my mouth will be close to the water, and I can drink all the time.' Finally he had drunk so much that he lost consciousness. Thus the water got even with Coyote for kicking it; and thus from a few drops of water originated the Columbia River.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 66 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and the Rain: Wishing a River

region.en: South of the Columbia River, dry coulee country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞河以南，乾谷之地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected on the Okanagon River; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (2b) Coyote and the Water or Rain' (Okanagon)

summary.en: Travelling hot and dry down a waterless coulee, Coyote tries resting in the shade of a rock and a tree, but both crack and lean over him and he flees. He wishes for a cloud — one comes; for many clouds — the sky overcasts; for rain — a little falls; for much rain — it pours; for a creek to cool his feet — one runs; then for a river to drink easily — and the river rises to his chin and carries him away to a distant country, where he floats ashore exhausted, and the ravens, crows, magpies and buzzards come to feed on him, thinking he is dead, until he gets up and chases them away.
summary.zh: 郊狼行於無水乾谷，燥熱難當。先於巖蔭歇腳，巖裂傾之，逃；再憩樹蔭，樹鳴壓頂，又逃。乃許願求雲——雲至；求多雲——天陰；求雨——微雨；求大雨——傾盆；求溪潤足——溪成；求河暢飲——河水齊頸，竟將其捲往異鄉。飄至岸邊，力竭而臥；渡鴉、烏鴉、喜鵲、兀鷹誤以為其已死，群集啄之，他起身驅散之。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Once Coyote was travelling somewhere south of the Columbia River. He was going down a coulee in which there was no water; the weather was very hot, and he felt very hot and dry. He saw a large rock and said, 'I will rest in its shade'; but the rock began to crack and lean over, and Coyote became afraid and ran away. After a while he saw a tree and thought he would rest in its shade; but it began to creak and lean over, so he ran away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 66 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He looked at the sky, but saw no clouds, and said, 'I wish a cloud would come!' Soon a cloud came up and shaded him. 'That is not enough. I want many clouds.' Soon the sky became overcast, but it was still hot; then he wished for rain, and a little came. 'I want much rain.' It began to pour down. 'I want a creek, so that my feet may be cool' — a creek ran and he walked in it. 'That is not enough. I want a river, so that I may be cool and drink easily.' A river ran then, reached to his chin, and carried him away to a distant country, where he floated ashore quite exhausted and lay on the bank. The ravens, crows, magpies, and buzzards came to feed on him, thinking he was dead; he got up and chased them away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 66-67 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote Introduces the Salmon

region.en: Columbia River from its falls to Spokane (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 哥倫比亞河自瀑布至斯波坎（象徵定位）

texts.period: Told by Red-Arm (Nespelim/Lower Okanagon); collected by James A. Teit; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (3a) Introduction of Salmon' (Okanagon, told by Red-Arm)

summary.en: Flushed down his own wished-for river, Coyote drifts as a canoe to the weir of the two We'lwel sisters, who own all the salmon below the falls while the interior knows nothing of them. Taken up as a dish, filled with boiled salmon, the dish is discovered emptied; when the younger sister tries to smash it on a rock it becomes a crying baby, and they rear 'our younger brother' — who eats their stores, then breaks their weir under a horn-spoon helmet while they beat him in vain. The salmon run upstream to the Coyote people, the sisters are transformed into sandpipers, and up every river Coyote goes the salmon follow: he makes fishing-places for the people who treat him well and barriers for those who refuse him, leaving Spokane Falls half-dug because the people above would not give him a wife.
summary.zh: 郊狼為己所願之河沖走，化舟漂至 We'lwel 二姊妹之魚梁；彼等獨佔瀑布以下之鮭，內陸之人尚不識鮭味。姊妹取舟為盤盛熟鮭，鮭卻失蹤；妹怒欲碎盤於石，盤忽化啼嬰，遂收養為『小弟』——他偷食其存糧，並戴羊角勺盔頂拆魚梁，棒擊無效。鮭遂上溯至郊狼子孫之地；二姊化為鷸鳥。此後郊狼行至何處，鮭隨至何處：善待其者得漁場，拒婚者得石障；斯波坎瀑布即因上方之人不許婚而半途停工之坑。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon/Nespelim narrative told by Red-Arm and recorded by Teit (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Salmon-liberation culture-hero cycle; the Similkameen variant (3b) with franker content was not separately cut. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a large river, and Coyote floated along in it. After drifting a long time he regained consciousness, and when he discovered himself in the middle of a large, swift-running river he became afraid and changed himself into a small canoe. Away down below, somewhere above the place where Portland is now, where there is a fall in the river, there lived the two We'lwel sisters, who owned a weir that extended across the stream. Below the weir the river was full of salmon, while above it, in the interior, there were none: the Indians there knew nothing of salmon at that time, and lived on game, roots, and berries. Coyote, still in the form of a canoe bottom up, struck the weir and remained there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 67 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the morning the sisters came out to clean the weir of driftwood, and saw the small canoe bottom up. The younger said, 'We must save it. It will make a fine dish to hold our salmon in'; the elder said, 'Do not touch it. It has been made by some one. Possibly it is Coyote.' The younger took it home and put boiled salmon into it, and when they returned from root-digging the salmon in the dish had disappeared, and also some of the fish they had been drying. The younger sister became angry and tried to break the dish on a rock; as she was about to do so, the dish assumed the shape of a baby and began to cry, and she took pity: 'Oh, he will make a nice younger brother for us!' Coyote grew fast; tied up when they went root-digging, he unfastened himself and ate their roots and dried salmon, tying himself up again before they returned. 'How good our younger brother is!' the women would say.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 67 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote planned to break the women's weir and let the salmon pass up river. The fourth day, when the elder sister's root-digger broke and something felt wrong, they hastened home — meanwhile Coyote had put a sheep's-horn spoon on his head and was breaking the weir. They rushed at him and beat him over the head with sticks, but he kept on working faster than ever, the horn spoon protecting him. When the weir was broken, he ran up the opposite bank, and the king-salmon were ascending the river in great numbers. The sisters sat down on the bank and wept: 'You have stolen our salmon for your Coyote people! You are all Coyote people! You are bad people!' He answered, 'You thought you had a little boy, a little brother. You thought he knew nothing, but he was greater than you!' Then he transformed them into birds — sandpipers — saying, 'Henceforth you shall run by the water's edge. You shall no longer have control over salmon. Salmon shall henceforth run up the river.' The place where the weir was is now a fall in the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 67-68 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote walked along the river-bank, and the salmon followed him. Hungry, he wished the king-salmon to jump ashore; on rocky and clayey banks the slimy fish slipped back, but the fourth time it jumped on a sandy shore and he caught it. He cooked and ate his fill, then carried the rest on his back, asking a girl at every camp to marry him — all refused. At the mouth of the Similkameen he left the salmon and went up alone; the people there refused him because he was ugly, so he said, 'You shall have plenty of sheep, but salmon you shall not have. You will have to travel long distances to obtain your salmon,' and made a barrier so no salmon ascend the Similkameen. Above the Okanagon falls the people did not want him, and he made a rock barrier there. At Kali'tcamen the old people wanted to marry their daughters to him; he made a fine salmon-fishing place there, contracting the river and smoothing the rocks so children could play on them, and made a salmon-weir — then learned the girls would not have him, and kicked the weir to pieces. But he thought, 'The girl alone is bad; it is not the old people's fault. They were good to me,' and left the place as he had made it, where people have always been able to capture salmon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 68-69 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Nespe'lim Creek and at Hi'tcox near Spoke'in the same happened: the people accepted him, the girl refused him, and he had pity on the old people — 'There shall always be some salmon here,' he said. At Snuxami'na he threw half a cooked salmon into the river, where it became a rock like the side of a king-salmon. At Ski'tco, where the town of Spokane now is, he found a barrier across the stream and began to dig it away; but when he thought, 'Perhaps the people above are bad and will not give me a wife. Why should I favor them?' he went and saw the people who refused him, and left the hole the way it was: it forms now Spokane Falls, and not many salmon go up there, therefore the Coeur d'Alene have no salmon. At Tqemi'p the leavings of a cooked salmon became rocks forming an eddy, where, he said, some salmon of the first run will always die. At Colville the Wolverene people had ordered two of their daughters to marry him for the sake of fine food, and he filled their weir with king-salmon every morning; near there he made a dam and showed the people the methods of fishing with dip-nets and spears.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 69-70 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and the Steelhead-Salmon Sisters

region.en: Winter ice of the Columbia, great fishing-station (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 冬季哥倫比亞河冰面，大漁場（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected in the Okanagon country; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (3c) Coyote and the Steelhead-Salmon' (Okanagon)

summary.en: Walking the winter ice, Coyote doubles back to meet the two Steelhead sisters and proposes a wrestle, intending to throw the elder; instead she hurls him on the ice so hard that it kills him. He lies drying to bones and skin until Fox hears of his death and jumps over his bones — Coyote comes to life, sits up, yawns, and says he only lay down for a nap. Ever since, that stretch of the river has been a good place for steelhead, where the Indians catch numbers in springtime; it became one of the great fishing-stations of the Columbia, for Coyote is said to have turned back from there, and not many salmon go above it.
summary.zh: 郊狼冬日行於冰面，折返欲戲鋼頭鱒二姊妹，假意摔跤以圖不軌；孰料姊姊將其重摔於冰上，竟斃命。屍身日久風乾，僅餘皮骨；狐聞其死訊，躍過其骨，郊狼遂活，坐起哈欠道：『吾不過臥此小憩。』自此該段河道多鋼頭鱒，春日漁獲甚豐，成哥倫比亞大漁場之一——相傳郊狼至此折返，故其上鮭魚不多。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling along the ice of the river. It was wintertime. He saw the two Steelhead sisters on the ice, and said, 'I will go back, meet them, and fool them.' When they met, the elder sister recognized him, and said, 'Halloo, Coyote! Where are you going? What do you want?' He answered, 'Oh, I am just travelling along on the ice! Yes, I want something. I wish to wrestle with you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 71-72 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: They wrestled, and the woman threw him upon the ice so hard that it killed him. He lay there a long time, and dried up, until only his bones and skin remained. Fox heard of his death, and jumped over his bones; Coyote came to life, sat up, and yawned. He said, 'I just lay down here and had a nap.' Fox said, 'You were dead a long time, and I have brought you to life.' Ever since that time this part of the river has been a good place for steelhead-fish, and the Indians catch numbers there in the springtime. This place became one of the great fishing-stations on the Columbia; not many salmon go above it, for Coyote is said to have turned back from there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 72 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and the Ice People

region.en: House of ice in the snowy north (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 北地冰雪之屋（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected in the Okanagon country; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (5) Coyote and the Ice People' (Okanagon)

summary.en: The three Ice or Cold people kill Indians with cold weather, cold winds and ice, and love the cold; many have died at their hands. Coyote consults his excrements, who teach him their secret names and a plan: his three droppings become fresh service-berries (a gift), the heat of the sun to melt their house, and dead pine-needles (ka'ma). Addressed as a relative, admitted as one of the Ice people, he complains of the heat while the ice house melts and drips; outside, he fires the pine-needles he left at the door and burns the house down, killing Cold and his wife. The daughter escapes — had Coyote caught her too, there would be no cold or ice in the world now — and he transforms her: 'Henceforth you shall be known as Cold, but you shall not be able to kill people, excepting once in a while an exhausted hunter.'
summary.zh: 冰族三口以嚴寒冰雪殺人，且酷愛寒冷；斃命其手者眾。郊狼問計於己糞，得其所授密名與計策：三次所遺糞便分別化為鮮 service-莓（禮物）、融冰之陽光、以及易燃之枯松針（ka'ma）。他以親戚之名入其冰屋，被視為同族；他佯稱屋內酷熱，冰屋漸融滴漏。出屋後點燃入門時所留松針，四面縱火，冰屋焚燬，寒夫婦斃命，唯女逃逸——若郊狼亦擒之，世間將再無冰雪——遂化之為寒：『自此汝名為寒，然不得殺人，唯偶爾奪疲憊獵人之命。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Cold-monster-slaying culture-hero episode. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling, and came near to where the Ice people lived. They killed Indians by means of cold weather, cold winds, and ice; they loved the cold, and many people had been killed by them. Coyote determined to kill them, but did not know how; he defecated and asked his excrements what he should do. They told him, 'The three Ice or Cold people are very powerful. When you reach their house, you must address them as relatives. Call the man brother-in-law; when you address them, call the husband xwexwens-takain, the wife xwixwemkellks, and the daughter le'luaken.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 74 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: There was much snow on the ground, and the weather was very cold. Coyote defecated three times, and asked each piece of dung what it would be. The first said, 'I shall be fresh service-berries; the Ice people give berries to their daughter.' The second said, 'I shall be heat of the sun, which will soon melt the ice; when it begins to drip, say your house is very hot, then open your shirt and blow on your body.' The last said, 'I shall be ka'ma' — dead yellow pine-needles. When Coyote reached the house of these people he was nearly frozen; he went in and acted as directed. The Ice people said, 'This man must be a relative. He knows our names and all we do. Besides, nobody ever came in here without dying. He must be one of the Ice people.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 74 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote surprised them by complaining of the heat. Before long the ice of the house began to melt and drip; Coyote opened his shirt and blew on his body, saying, 'What a hot house you have!' The Ice people danced and sang and blew to make it colder, but the house continued to melt. 'I cannot stand the heat,' he said, went outside, set fire to the dead yellow pine-needles he had left at the door, and threw the burning needles all over the outside of the house while the heat of the sun melted it from within.
