Soon it was burned, and Cold and his wife were killed by the heat; their daughter rushed out and escaped. Had Coyote succeeded in catching her too, there would have been no cold or ice in the world now. Coyote transformed her, saying, 'Henceforth you shall be known as Cold, but you shall not be able to kill people, excepting once in a while an exhausted hunter.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 74 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote Visits the Blackfeet

region.en: Eastern foot-hills of the Rocky Mountains, Blackfoot country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 落基山東麓，黑腳族故地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected in the Okanagon country; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (6) Coyote and the Blackfeet' (Okanagon)

summary.en: Coyote, who has no relatives to mourn him, goes east to see the fighting people; ashamed to arrive alone, he asks his excrements — threatening to dry them up — until they turn three droppings into twenty horses, fine clothes and a fine head of hair. The Blackfeet receive the 'great chief' and keep his gift-horses; but when his wife, angry at his scolding, strikes his pinto with a stone, it turns to excrement, he falls into the filth, and the people strike camp, leaving the gift horses at their stakes to become dung where they stand.
summary.zh: 郊狼自知死後無親可泣，遂東行往觀好戰之民。恥於孤身赴會，乃問計於己糞，並以乾死相脅；三枚糞塊遂化為駿馬二十、華服一套、美髯一束。黑腳族人奉為『大酋長』，厚待三日，並留其所贈之馬。第三日，其妻怒其惡言，以石擊其花馬——馬化為糞，郊狼墜入穢中；族人拔營而去，所贈之馬盡留樁旁，原地化糞。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote's wife was the Short-Tailed Mouse. He said to her, 'Wife, I have no relatives to cry and feel sorry if I die. I am going to see the people on the Plains, who do much fighting.' He went to the Blackfoot country, and when he reached the eastern foot-hills of the Rocky Mountains, he saw from the edge of a hill great numbers of people with horses pitching tents. He said to his wife, 'I am ashamed to go among these people alone.' He defecated three times and asked his excrements what to do; they said, 'You are bothering us again.' Coyote spat in the air and said, 'If you do not answer me quickly, you will dry up and die' — and his excrements became afraid and answered at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 75-76 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The first piece said, 'I shall be a band of twenty horses'; the second, 'I shall be fine clothes'; the last, 'I shall be a fine head of hair.' Coyote put on the fine clothes and fine hair, and mounted his wife on a large pinto horse. The Blackfeet saw him coming and said, 'Here is a great chief coming to visit us.' He gave most of his horses as presents to the chiefs, stopped three days, and was well entertained. On the third day he told his wife, 'Be very careful not to throw any stones at our horses'; but that day his wife became angry at his talking nastily to her, and struck his horse with a stone — immediately it turned into excrement, and he fell down in the midst of it, stuck there up to his waist. Now the people found him out: 'It is Coyote.' They struck camp and left him still cleaning himself of the filth, leaving at their stakes the horses he had given them — and there they became excrement.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 76 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote, Fox, and Panther: The Bride Who Howled
title.zh: 郊狼、狐狸與山君：夜半狼嚎的新娘

region.en: Okanagon Lake villages, British Columbia (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 奧卡諾根湖村落，不列顛哥倫比亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected at Okanagon Lake; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Okanagon Tales, (7) Coyote, Fox, and Panther' (Okanagon, from Okanagon Lake)

summary.en: Fox's luck fails and the friends starve; urged three days to break the spell, Coyote at last washes, dresses his hair and paints his face like a woman, and goes to Panther's village as a bride sent by her parents. Panther agrees to wait; Coyote carries three packs of food home to his starving brother Fox. Wise Prairie-Chicken tells the people their chief's bride is Coyote, and as the sweat-house gathering is about to reveal it, Coyote runs above, howls like a coyote, and shouts the taunt — 'You will never have a good wife, Panther, you bad warrior, you bad man of the warpath!' — and Panther is too ashamed to speak.
summary.zh: 狐運蹇獵空，二友斷糧；三日催促郊狼破咒無果，郊狼忽洗浴梳妝敷粉如女子，投山君（Panther）部落，自稱父母許嫁而來。山君守禮待之；郊狼則三日三擔食物送回家中餵狐。智鳥草原雞識破，告眾：『酋長新婦非女子，乃郊狼也！』眾人正欲於汗屋中道破，郊狼繞屋嚎叫如狼，揚聲嘲罵：『山君惡徒！戰陣懦夫！汝永不會得好妻！』山君羞愧無言。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of an Okanagon narrative (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote and Fox were living together. They were friends, and always had plenty to eat, for Fox was a good hunter. Once upon a time he had bad luck, and could not get any game — perhaps he had been bewitched — and the friends began to starve. Fox said to Coyote, 'You are powerful and gifted. Try to break our spell of bad luck, so that we may procure game.' Coyote did not answer; for three days Fox repeated his request, thinking, 'Coyote will do something foolish.' The fourth night Fox spoke again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 75-76 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Early the following morning Coyote arose, went to wash himself at a spring near by, returned to the lodge, and drew from under his pillow his comb and paint-pouch. Without speaking, he dressed his hair and painted his face after the manner of women, then dressed himself and left the house. He travelled about aimlessly until he came to the houses of many people, whose chief was Panther, and sat down alongside of him. 'I do not come here for nothing, chief. My father and mother sent me here to marry you.' Panther answered, 'I do not desire to act contrary to the pleasure of your parents. I will not decline their offer, if they have chosen me as their son-in-law.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 76 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Night came, and Panther asked Coyote to go to bed with him; but Coyote drew away, saying, 'I am a maiden and have never known man. I am afraid and ashamed. I am also thinking of my parents. If you will give me a pack of food to take to my parents three successive days, I will be yours.' Panther agreed, and on the following morning Coyote carried a pack of food to his starving younger brother. Prairie-Chicken, who was a wise person, said to the others, 'Our chief is a great man, but he has made a grave mistake. His wife is not a woman, she is Coyote.' Now Prairie-Chicken and others made a sweat-house and invited Panther to sweat with them, intending to tell him who his wife really was and to purify him. When Panther was inside, Coyote ran about above the sweat-house and howled like a coyote, shouting, 'You will never have a good wife. Panther, you bad warrior, you bad man of the warpath!' Panther was ashamed, and said nothing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 76 (Teit, 1917); not verbatim.
